rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to capture all 6 compounds without truncation and map the overall elution window. The wide phi range and moderate slope should reveal whether peaks are early, late, or compressed, guiding later window and slope optimization.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only path to a better CRF is reducing t_last. The first run shows the full elution window sits well inside the gradient, so a narrower, steeper window with higher temperature should pull the last peak closer to 10 min while likely preserving ample resolution.

We are very close to the ideal, with all pairs still comfortably above 1.5, so the next step is to shorten the run slightly more and raise temperature one notch. This tests whether t_last can be pushed under 10 min while keeping the current closest pair resolved.

CRF is already maxed, so use the remaining budget to see whether an even faster method still keeps the limiting pair above 1.5. This is a controlled push steeper and hotter from the current optimum to probe the minimum safe runtime.

The 6 min method is fast enough, but resolution failure shifted to the first pair, suggesting temperature rather than overall slope is the key lever. Dropping T one step while keeping the same short gradient tests whether we can recover full resolution and retain t_last well under 10 min.

Now that 6 min at 55 C gives full resolution with margin, the next optimization is trimming the high-organic end because the last peak likely does not need phi1 as high as 0.70. A slightly narrower window can preserve or even improve selectivity while staying fast and fully within the gradient.

Lowering phi1 slowed the last peak, so the best direction for faster analysis is the opposite: raise phi1 one step above 0.70 while keeping the proven 6 min, 55 C conditions. This should test whether we can further shorten the late elution without sacrificing the still-safe early-pair resolution.

The trend from phi1 0.65 to 0.75 shows higher phi1 shortens t_last while resolution remains acceptable, with the first pair still above 1.5. Pushing phi1 one more step tests the fastest high-organic window likely to retain full resolution before that early pair starts to fail.

Increasing phi1 continues to reduce t_last, and the limiting first pair is only gradually weakening, so one more step should locate the upper edge before resolution drops below 1.5. This is the most direct way to identify the fastest fully resolved method on the current grid.

At phi1 0.85 the critical first pair is just above the 1.5 threshold, so one final step higher should determine whether that is the upper limit for a 6 min method. If it fails, phi1 0.85 is confirmed as the fastest fully resolved condition explored so far.

Phi1 0.85 appears to be the fastest fully resolved setting so far; now test whether raising phi0 can further compress the run without losing the first pair. Because the critical pair elutes very early, this is risky but informative and could reveal a still faster max-CRF method.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 preserved full resolution while keeping the critical pair just above threshold, so the next fastest test is to pair that higher phi0 with phi1 0.90. This checks whether the same balance can hold at a stronger upper endpoint, potentially beating the current fastest fully resolved method.

The first pair remains the limiting constraint, and phi0 = 0.10, phi1 = 0.85 still clears it by a small margin. Testing phi0 one step higher at the same phi1 probes whether additional front-end compression can still preserve full resolution while edging toward the shortest viable method.

The fastest fully resolved region is clearly bounded by the first pair, and temperature strongly affects that pair. This run tests whether a hotter method with a slightly less aggressive phi1 can still maintain full resolution while potentially matching or beating the current short max-CRF candidates.

Since higher temperature hurts the critical first pair, test the opposite direction at the current fastest fully resolved composition. Lowering T one step from 55 to 50 should strengthen the limiting pair and shows whether 55 C is really needed for this 6 min, high-phi1 method.

At 50 C the limiting first pair gained substantial resolution margin, so it is worth revisiting phi1 0.90 under the cooler condition. This could deliver a faster fully resolved run than the 55 C version, which failed only narrowly on the first pair.

At 50 C the critical first pair still has comfortable margin at phi1 0.90, so the next logical boundary test is phi1 0.95. This may identify an even faster fully resolved 6 min method and defines the high-end limit of phi1 under the cooler condition.

Phi1 0.95 at 50 C is fully resolved with good margin on the first pair, so raising phi0 to 0.10 is the next way to compress the run further. This tests whether the current fastest high-phi1 condition can be improved while staying above the 1.5 resolution threshold.

The current 0.10 to 0.95, 6 min, 50 C method still has comfortable margin on the critical first pair, so one more increase in phi0 is justified. This probes whether the run can be compressed even further while remaining fully resolved.

The first pair still has a clear buffer at phi0 0.15, phi1 0.95, so increasing phi0 another step is the most direct way to seek an even shorter fully resolved method. This continues to map the front-end limit while keeping the proven strong upper endpoint and cooler temperature.

The front-end limit is now clear at 50 C, with phi0 0.20 failing and phi0 0.15 succeeding; the next useful boundary test is whether 55 C can hold full resolution at the same fast 0.15 to 0.95 window. This checks whether a slightly hotter variant might still be viable or confirms 50 C as the safer optimum.

Among the fastest fully resolved methods, 0.15 to 0.95 at 6 min and 50 C is strongest so far; with the remaining budget, the main unresolved question is the shortest safe tG. Lengthening to 8 min at the same composition confirms the slope sensitivity of the limiting first pair and brackets 6 min as likely the minimum fully resolved gradient.

The remaining useful boundary is gradient time: 6 min is fully resolved and 8 min only adds excess margin, so a 4 min test at a slightly safer phi0 than 0.15 probes whether an even shorter max-CRF method exists. Using phi0 0.10 preserves extra space for the critical first pair while keeping the strongest upper endpoint and favorable temperature.

The 4 min test failed because the first pair collapsed, so the cleanest rescue is to lower phi0 one step while keeping the same fast tG, high phi1, and favorable temperature. This directly tests whether a 4 min fully resolved method is still possible if more retention is restored for the earliest pair.

The data show 6 min is the shortest safe gradient, phi1 0.95 is beneficial, and the limiting first pair improves at lower temperature. With one shot left, dropping from 50 to 45 C at the fastest fully resolved composition tests for an even more robust final method while staying comfortably under 10 min.
